At the corner shop Leela pointed at the jar of toffees. "Not today," said her mother Kamal. Leela's scream came from somewhere deep in her belly. She dropped on the floor, kicked her feet and felt her whole body get too big to hold. Kamal crouched beside her. "No toffees today, and I know that is hard. Let's breathe like we're blowing out a birthday candle." She breathed slowly, in and out, until Leela's kicking slowed and she leaned on her knee, hiccupping.

On Tuesday it was the same jar of toffees, but her father Gautam had come from a long, loud day. Leela began to wail. "Stop that right now or there'll be no park for a week!" he shouted, his face hard. Leela's crying stopped as if a lid had closed. Her hands went cold and she stared at his shoes. She was not thinking about toffees or why the answer was no. She was thinking, Papa is scary.

That evening Gautam knelt down beside her bed. "I shouted and I frightened you, and I'm sorry. Big feelings are allowed. The answer about toffees is still no, but we can share an apple." Leela climbed into his arms and stayed there.

qa.q: What did Leela point at in the corner shop?
qa.a: She pointed at the jar of toffees.

qa.q: How did Leela's tantrum feel to her, and how was it different when Gautam shouted instead of Kamal staying calm?
qa.a: When Leela screamed, her body felt too big and Kamal stayed calm, kept the limit and helped her breathe, so she slowly settled. When Gautam shouted and threatened, she went quiet out of fear and did not think about the limit at all.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when her crying stopped after Gautam shouted?
qa.a: She was frightened, since her hands went cold and she was thinking that Papa was scary.

qa.q: What could Gautam do the next time Leela has a tantrum when he is tired?
qa.a: He could stay calm, keep the limit about toffees, help her breathe and repair with a hug and an explanation afterwards if he does lose his temper.

grounding: A child's tantrum about being told no is seen from her own big feelings and from a frightening shout, with a calm response and a later repair.

passage:
In the canteen, Ganga leaned over her tea. "Promise you won't tell anyone, but Naveen didn't clear the placement round." Vasudha's eyes widened, and Ganga felt the small glow of being the one who knew. By evening the glow had gone sour. Someone in the hostel corridor said, "Sorry about placements, Naveen." Ganga's stomach dropped when she saw his face.

Naveen had told only one person. His ears rang, he felt suddenly naked in the corridor, and for an hour he was so angry that he typed out a list of things Ganga had once said to him in private. His thumb hovered, then he deleted every line. He wrote, "Can we talk somewhere quiet?"

Ganga came before he could change his mind. She did not wait for him to speak. "I told Vasudha. I wanted to seem important, and that was wrong. I have no excuse. You can be angry." Naveen kept his arms folded. "I need some space, and I'll decide what's left between us." Ganga nodded and did not argue. The next week she noticed that she thought twice before repeating anything at all.

qa.q: What did Ganga tell Vasudha in the canteen?
qa.a: She told Vasudha that Naveen had not cleared the placement round.

qa.q: How did Ganga's and Naveen's views of the same leak differ, and what did each do about it?
qa.a: Ganga felt the glow of knowing then a sinking stomach, so she owned it and apologised with no excuse. Naveen felt exposed and furious, held back from leaking her secrets, and asked to talk privately, then asked for space.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling in the corridor when he heard the sorry about placements?
qa.a: He felt exposed and furious, as though everyone had seen something private.

qa.q: What could Ganga do in the weeks after Naveen asked for space?
qa.a: She could give him the distance he asked for without pressing, and be more careful with what others tell her.

grounding: One leaked confidence is shown from the friend who told it and from the friend whose secret spread.

passage:
Shalini watched Jeevan's name light up Eshaan's phone on the sofa arm and felt her stomach tighten. For days she had asked, in a light voice, "Who were you texting?" and "Why so long?" Her hand drifted toward the phone when he showered. She stopped herself. What she wanted was not the messages. It was the small cold feeling underneath.

Eshaan had noticed every one of the questions. He answered them at first, cheerfully, then with a tired patience. He felt watched in his own home and a little resentful, though he had done nothing but text an old friend. "I've told you, there's nothing," he said. "I'll say it once more, but I can't hand over my phone every night."

That Sunday Shalini set the tea down. "I'm not accusing you. I feel insecure when Jeevan's name comes up and I don't know why. Could you help me feel less alone with it?" Eshaan's shoulders dropped. "Yes," he said. "But if this keeps going, I want us to talk to someone together. I don't want to feel checked on."

Shalini nodded slowly, and did not reach for his phone.

qa.q: Whose name lit up Eshaan's phone on the sofa arm?
qa.a: Jeevan's name lit up the phone.

qa.q: How did Shalini's questions and Eshaan's replies look from each side, and what changed on Sunday?
qa.a: Shalini felt a cold insecurity and kept asking questions, while Eshaan felt watched and resentful even though he had done nothing. On Sunday she said plainly that she felt insecure, and he offered reassurance while naming a limit.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as the questions kept coming?
qa.a: He felt watched and a little resentful, though he answered patiently at first.

qa.q: What could Shalini and Eshaan do if the insecurity comes back next month?
qa.a: Shalini can keep voicing the feeling instead of checking his phone, and they can talk to a counsellor together as Eshaan suggested.

grounding: A spouse's jealousy of a partner's friend is seen from the one feeling insecure and from the one who feels watched.

passage:
Ujjwal put a reminder in his phone for Nitin's practical exam, and on the morning itself he was outside the lab with a flask of tea and no speech. He did not post about it. When friends pushed for an anniversary reel, he said, "We'll keep it small." Weeks earlier, when Nitin admitted he was scared of getting too serious this early, Ujjwal had not sulked. "Tell me when it feels heavy," he had said, and Nitin had told him.

Nitin, for his part, felt chosen, and it was warm and slightly frightening at the same time. Someone had decided on him, out loud, and would keep turning up. He wanted to be worth it and was not sure he could promise everything. "I might get it wrong sometimes," he told Ujjwal on the terrace. "I'm still figuring out who I am." Ujjwal shrugged and smiled. "Then figure it out. I'll be here."

On Saturday, Nitin still went to his football game with Yusuf and the others, and Ujjwal enrolled in a Saturday photography class he had wanted for years. That night Nitin thanked him. "I noticed the tea. I don't want to take it for granted."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal bring to Nitin's practical exam?
qa.a: He brought a flask of tea.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal's steady actions and Nitin's response show the two sides of the same relationship?
qa.a: Ujjwal showed love by turning up, listening and making room for Nitin, without a show for others. Nitin felt chosen, both warm and frightening, so he was honest about his limits, kept his football with Yusuf and thanked Ujjwal.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he thought about someone deciding on him out loud?
qa.a: He felt warm and a little scared, wanting to be worthy without promising too much.

qa.q: What could Nitin do if he starts to take Ujjwal's steady support for granted?
qa.a: He could keep noticing the small things, like the tea, and thank Ujjwal while still keeping his own friendships and honesty.

grounding: Committed love is seen from the partner who chooses steadily and from the partner who feels chosen and a little frightened.

passage:
Ramesh had cancelled dinner with Hansa's parents to finish a work deadline, and she said "fine" in a voice like a closed door. For the next two days she answered only with nods. Saying that she was hurt felt too exposed, and going cold felt like a way to make him feel it. Her friend Aparna asked on the phone, "Have you told him you're upset?" Hansa said, "He should know."

Ramesh moved around the flat on tiptoe, his chest tight. He kept checking what he might have done and started drafting an apology for everything. Then he stopped. "I don't want to guess," he told himself, and on the third evening he sat across from her. "Hansa, I can tell something is wrong. I'm not going to grovel or guess. When you're ready, I want to hear it. Going quiet to make me pay hurts us both."

Hansa looked at her hands. After a long moment she said, "I'm upset that you cancelled on my parents without asking me. I need a bit of time tonight, and then I want to talk." Ramesh nodded, and made her tea.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh cancel dinner with Hansa's parents?
qa.a: He cancelled to finish a work deadline.

qa.q: How did Hansa's silence look from her side, and how did it feel to Ramesh?
qa.a: For Hansa, going cold felt safer than admitting she was hurt. For Ramesh, the silence brought worry, guilt and a wish to fix everything, until he invited her to talk without guessing his crime.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling while he moved around the flat on tiptoe?
qa.a: He felt anxious and guilty, with a tight chest, and he badly wanted to fix things.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time she is upset with Ramesh instead of going silent?
qa.a: She could say plainly that she is upset and needs a little time, as she finally did, and then talk.

grounding: A partner's punishing silence is seen from the one who goes cold to hide hurt and the one left anxious and guilty.

passage:
Arohi had spent all afternoon on her drawing of a green elephant. Then her brother Tenzin, wanting to add colour, dragged a red crayon across it and tore the paper. Heat rose through her chest and arms. She shoved him and hit his shoulder, hard.

Tenzin stumbled backward and sat on the floor. Arohi was bigger and louder, and he felt tiny. His arm hurt and his eyes filled, and he felt he had no way to make it stop. He ran to the kitchen. "Amma, Arohi pushed me!"

Aadhya, their mother, turned off the stove and came straight over. She checked Tenzin's arm first, then knelt by both children. "Nobody hits in this house. Arohi, tell me what happened. Tenzin, you too." Arohi crossed her arms. Then, with a shaky voice, she said, "He broke my elephant, and I am mad!" Aadhya nodded. "That's a good thing to say with words. Hitting was not okay." She sent Arohi to sit for a few minutes with her drawing, and helped Tenzin fetch tape. Tenzin was still a bit cross that Arohi had pushed, and did not want to share his crayons.

qa.q: What was Arohi drawing?
qa.a: She was drawing a green elephant.

qa.q: How did the drawing fight look from Arohi's side and from Tenzin's side, and what did Aadhya do about both?
qa.a: Arohi felt hot anger and hit back, while Tenzin felt tiny and hurt and ran to tell their mother. Aadhya checked Tenzin, listened to both, and asked for words instead of hitting, while giving Arohi a few quiet minutes.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he sat on the floor after being pushed?
qa.a: He felt tiny and helpless, with his arm hurting and his eyes filling.

qa.q: What could Arohi do next time Tenzin damages something she made?
qa.a: She could say, "You broke it, I'm mad," and get her mother, as she managed to do this time, instead of hitting.

grounding: One broken drawing is seen from the sibling who hits back in anger and from the sibling who is pushed and turns to a parent.
